item.title: Accelerating inverse materials design using generative diffusion models with reinforcement learning
item.description:
Nature Machine Intelligence · Junwu Chen, Jeff Guo, Edvin Fako, Philippe Schwaller
Diffusion models promise to accelerate materials design by directly generating novel structures with desired properties, but existing approaches such as conditional generation typically require expensive and substantial labelled data (>10,000) and lack adaptability. Here we present MatInvent, a general and efficient reinforcement learning workflow that optimizes diffusion models for goal-directed crystal generation. By formulating equivariant denoising as a multistep decision-making problem, MatInvent leverages policy gradient with reward-weighted Kullback–Leibler regularization, including experience replay and diversity filters to enhance optimization efficiency and sample diversity. For single-objective designs, MatInvent rapidly converges to target values within 60 iterations (~1,000 property evaluations) across electronic, magnetic, mechanical, thermal and physicochemical properties. Furthermore, MatInvent achieves robust optimization in design tasks with multiple conflicting properties, successfully proposing low-supply-chain-risk magnets and high- κ dielectrics. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, MatInvent exhibits comparable or superior generation performance under specified property constraints while markedly reducing the demand for property computation. Compatible with diverse diffusion model architectures and property constraints, MatInvent could offer broad applicability in materials discovery.

item.title: A measurement noise scaling law for cellular representation learning
item.description:
Nature Machine Intelligence · gokul gowri, Igor Sadalski, Dan Raviv, Peng Yin, Jonathan Rosenfeld, Allon Moshe Klein
Large genomic and imaging datasets can be used to train models that learn meaningful representations of cellular systems. Across domains, model performance improves predictably with dataset size and compute budget, providing a basis for allocating data and computation. Scientific data, however, are also limited by noise arising from factors such as molecular undersampling, sequencing errors and image resolution. Here we introduce mutual information with auxiliary signals as a metric of representation model performance and study its scaling with noise. By fitting more than 2,000 representation learning models across three data modalities (gene expression, sequence and image data), we show that noise defines a distinct axis along which performance improves. Noise scaling follows a logarithmic law. We derive the law from a model of noise propagation, and use it to define noise sensitivity and model capacity as benchmarking metrics. We show that protein-sequence representations tolerate error rates in modern sequencing data, whereas single-cell transcriptomic models remain noise limited at current measurement signal-to-noise ratio levels. Within transcriptomic cell-state representation learning models, we find that transformer-based models are more noise robust but less performant than variational autoencoders. Noise scaling metrics may support future model evaluation and experimental design.

item.title: Development and clinical validation of a multimodal AI framework to predict persistent fever during antibiotic therapy in hospitalized patients with cancer
item.description:
Nature Communications · Gernot Pucher, Kevin Kopp, Aman Deep, Anna-Maria Stark, Marcel Wiesweg, Martin Schuler
Among hospitalized cancer patients, persistent fever despite intravenous antibiotics often triggers treatment escalation and additional diagnostics. Earlier identification of patients at low risk for ongoing fever could support more selective decision-making. We developed and compared multimodal AI frameworks to predict persistent fever at the 48–72-hour reassessment window. Models integrated structured variables, time-series, notes, and chest imaging. Models were developed in a University Hospital Essen cohort and evaluated using holdout validation, two pooled regional hospitals, and MIMIC-IV ICU. A feature-level tabularized multimodal TabPFN model showed consistent discrimination, with AUC 0.84 (95% CI, 0.81–0.86) in cross-validation, 0.82 (95% CI, 0.77–0.87) in holdout validation, and 0.78 (95% CI, 0.74–0.81) in MIMIC-IV; other multimodal strategies showed comparable but more variable performance. Performance was primarily driven by temperature dynamics, while chest-radiograph imaging provided no incremental predictive value. In a clinician validation study, the multimodal model outperformed clinicians (Trial 1 balanced accuracy: 0.77 vs 0.60; Trial 2: 0.79 vs 0.57), while clinician balanced accuracy reached 0.71 (95% CI 0.67–0.75) in the AI-assisted condition, suggesting potential benefit of AI support. Overall, multimodal AI demonstrates potential to support 48-hour antibiotic reassessment and stewardship-oriented decision-making, although further prospective studies are needed.

item.title: Scalable 3D hybrid integrated photonic computing chiplets
item.description:
Nature Communications · Hang Song, Chao-Qian Li, Yun-Long Nie, Yu-Xuan Fu, De-Hui Huang, Yi Xie
The exponential surge in artificial intelligence computing power demand is driving a transition from electrons to photons across the infrastructure. Although integrated photonics has revolutionized communications and computing, its scaling for large-scale information processing is constrained by monolithic scalability, modulation efficiency, and multi-chip integration. Here, we present HyPec, a hybrid photonic extensible chiplet architecture that synergizes thin-film lithium niobate modulation chiplets with femtosecond laser-written three-dimensional functional chiplets. Through function disaggregation, HyPec partitions high-performance active modulation from the 3D photonic routing network. This chiplet architecture facilitates seamless multi-chip connectivity across diverse material platforms to achieve aggregate performance beyond monolithic limits, thereby allowing the system to scale through the addition of functional chiplets. To validate the advantages of this architecture, we experimentally built a co-packaged photonic computing chiplet system that implements a scalable graph solver and further identifies critical protein residues in structural biology networks. This work establishes a scalable hardware path for integrated photonic computing, with broader implications for high-density optical interconnects and photonic quantum information systems.

item.title: EcoVAE: a generative deep learning method for global species distribution prediction
item.description:
Nature Communications · Yujing Yan, Bin Shao, Jiawei Yan, Charles “Chuck” Davis
Anthropogenic pressures on biodiversity necessitate efficient and scalable methods to predict global species distributions. Current species distribution models (SDMs) face challenges with large-scale datasets, complex species associations, and data quality. Here, we introduce EcoVAE, an autoencoder-based generative model that integrates bioclimatic variables with georeferenced occurrences. The model is trained separately for plants, butterflies, and mammals to predict global distributions at both genus and species levels. Through unsupervised learning, EcoVAE captures underlying distribution patterns from large-scale species occurrence data. It achieves high precision and speed, outperforming traditional SDMs in spatial block cross-validation. EcoVAE also reveals signatures of species associations that align with known prey-predator relationships. Taken together, these capacities enable the robust evaluation of global sampling efforts and interpolates distributions in data-limited regions, offering new applications for biodiversity exploration and monitoring.

item.title: A spectral-spatial interweaver for hyperdimensional photonic computing
item.description:
Nature Communications · Yun-Long Nie, Hang Song, De-Hui Huang, Yi Xie, Chao-Qian Li, Yu-Xuan Fu
Photonic computing offers high bandwidth, parallelism and energy efficiency for artificial intelligence (AI), yet its scalability remains limited by bulky optical components and immature optoelectronic integration. Here we present HyperON, a thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) hyperdimensional optical network built around a passive spectral-spatial interweaver and broadband wavelength-parallel modulators. The interweaver combines wavelength multiplexing with spatial replication in a log 2 P -stage network, delivering the full wavelength set to every spatial output without beam-combination loss. By interweaving P spectral channels with K spatial units, HyperON forms a unified P × K parallel computing framework, supporting O ( N 2 ) operations with only O ( N ) modulators, improving hardware efficiency and scalability. A 16 × 16 interweaver shows low-loss, broadband and highly uniform operation across 1523.40-1568.85 nm, with 1.30 dB average loss, 0.196 dB output-port variation and 0.414 dB cross-wavelength variation. The integrated wavelength-parallel modulators retain system-level bandwidths of 53-67 GHz after large-scale routing, while standalone devices exhibit bandwidths beyond 67 GHz. Together, these features enable the fabricated HyperON chip to deliver a projected peak throughput of 32.8 TMAC/s, with estimated energy and area efficiencies of 7.04 TMAC/s/W and 0.163 TMAC/s/mm 2 , respectively. Experimental demonstrations in image convolution, handwritten digit recognition, and 64-mode parallel computing confirm its high speed operation, versatility, and scalability for large-scale AI workloads.

item.title: LitMOF: An LLM Multi-Agent for Literature-Validated Metal-Organic Frameworks Database Correction and Expansion
item.description:
Nature Communications · Honghui Kim, Dohoon Kim, Jihan Kim
Metal–organic framework databases have grown rapidly through experimental deposition and large-scale literature extraction, yet recent analyses indicate that nearly half of their entries contain substantial structural errors. These errors propagate through high-throughput screening and machine-learning workflows, limiting the reliability of data-driven materials discovery. Repairing them is difficult because the necessary evidence is scattered across crystallographic files, synthesis descriptions, and the primary literature. Here we present LitMOF, a multi-agent framework driven by large language models that reads the original publication for each structure and cross-validates it against the deposited entry to repair errors. Applying LitMOF to the metal–organic framework subset of the Cambridge Structural Database, we assembled LitMOF-DB, a curated set of 189,567 computation-ready structures that includes 9,277 repaired entries, or 69.1% of the not-computation-ready structures in the latest CoRE MOF database. The system also recovered 8,771 synthesized but undeposited frameworks missing from existing resources. Using direct air capture screening as a case study, we show that structural errors distort predicted adsorption energies and CO 2 /H 2 O selectivity, which misranks materials, produces false positives, and omits high-performing candidates. This work offers a route toward self-correcting scientific databases and toward database curation driven by large language models.

item.title: QAMNet: Co-designing deep learning with complex-valued computing machines
item.description:
npj Artificial Intelligence · Marc Gong Bacvanski, Sri Krishna Vadlamani, Kfir Sulimany, Dirk Robert Englund
The energy consumption of inference has become critically important with the growing adoption of deep neural networks (DNNs). Analog optical neural networks (ONNs) can reduce the energy of matrix-vector multiplication below that of digital electronics. However, this promise is limited by digital-to-analog (DAC) conversion: even at low bit precision b , encoding the 2 b levels of weights and inputs into the analog domain requires specialized, power-hungry electronics. Quadrature-Amplitude Modulation (QAM), the dominant format in modern telecommunications, encodes information on both the in-phase and quadrature axes of a carrier. A consequence of this two-dimensional signaling is a quadratic O ( N 2 ) → O ( N ) saving in modulation energy over intensity-only modulation. Inspired by this advantage, we introduce QAMNet, an ONN architecture and hardware that fully utilizes the complex amplitude of light with QAM to achieve superior modulation-energy scaling. Using physics-based simulations of conventional telecommunications equipment, we show that QAMNet accelerates complex-valued DNNs with accuracies indistinguishable from digital hardware. Compared to standard ONNs, QAMNet ONNs: (1) attain higher accuracy above moderate total bit precision, (2) are more accurate above low energy budgets, and (3) are optimal when hardware bit precision is limited.

item.title: A multimodal ultrasound foundation model for diagnosis of unexplained lymphadenopathy
item.description:
Nature Communications · Ran Cao, Yangyang Zhu, Zhibin Zhu, Li Qiu, Lin Chen, Fei Ouyang
Unexplained lymphadenopathy (ULA) leads to delayed diagnosis and increases the risk of disease progression due to the absence of specific clinical symptoms and indicative medical history during early stages, thereby increasing reliance on invasive biopsy. Existing ultrasound artificial intelligence approaches mainly use single-modality static images, limiting their generalizability and clinical applicability. Here, we develop and validate a multimodal model integrating B-mode ultrasound, color Doppler flow imaging, ultrasound elastography, contrast-enhanced ultrasound videos, and clinical data for benign-malignant differentiation, etiologic stratification, and metastatic-origin prediction. This observational study includes both retrospective and prospective cohorts and uses a total of 154,740 multimodal keyframe images from 6,549 patients with pathologically confirmed lymphadenopathy across seven Chinese centers and 11 scanner manufacturers. The model shows robust performance across internal, external, device-heterogeneity, and reader study cohorts, outperforms senior radiologists across hierarchical tasks, and improves radiologists’ diagnostic performance across experience levels with model assistance, supporting its potential for noninvasive, efficient, and clinically aligned diagnosis of ULA.

item.title: Large language models' complicit responses to illicit instructions across socio-legal contexts
item.description:
Nature Communications · Xing Wang, Huiyuan Xie, Yiyan Wang, Chaojun Xiao, Huimin Chen, Holli Sargeant
Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks.

item.title: Enabling lab autonomy with reward functions and executable workflows

item.title: Chemist-aligned retrosynthesis by ensembling diverse inductive bias models
item.description:
Nature · Krzysztof Maziarz, Guoqing Liu, Felix Pultar, John Gardner, Tobias Gensch, Jean Helie
Chemical synthesis remains a bottleneck in the discovery and manufacture of functional small molecules 1–3 . Although artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted synthesis planning has proliferated in recent years, a detailed understanding of its failure modes has not been achieved, and models still struggle with predicting less frequent, yet strategically important reactions, as well as hallucinated, incorrect predictions misaligned with chemists’ expectations 4–12 . Here, we analyse the failure modes of the present-day AI models and propose RetroChimera: a frontier retrosynthesis model, built on two newly developed components with complementary inductive biases, integrated through a new, learning-based ensembling strategy. Through experiments across several orders of magnitude in data scale, we show RetroChimera outperforms leading baselines, demonstrating robustness outside the training data, as well as the ability to learn from very small numbers of examples per reaction class. Using both pairwise and pointwise setups, we find that organic chemists prefer predictions from RetroChimera over published reference reactions and over other AI models. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer and fine-tuning on internal datasets from two pharmaceutical companies, showing robust generalization under distribution shift. Our work demonstrates the viability of deep learning for accurate synthesis prediction in increasingly challenging regimes.

item.title: A defence-in-depth strategy for securing AI-driven biological sequence design
item.description:
Nature Communications · Maximilian Sprang, Hassan Abdullah Hassan, Yasha Ektefaie, Anne Schmieder, Alix Wasilenko, Moritz Hanke
Generative artificial intelligence can design biological sequences, from proteins to whole genomes, opening opportunities for medicine and biotechnology, but the same capability can be misused. The Wübben Sandpit conference brought together experts in biology, AI, biosecurity, ethics, medicine and policy to ask how the field can capture the benefits while managing the risks. Here we set out a defence-in-depth strategy that builds safeguards into every stage, from the data used to train models, to the models themselves, to the synthesis of physical DNA. We argue that responsible governance is not a brake on progress but a precondition for it. Generative artificial intelligence can design biological sequences, from proteins to whole genomes, however this capability can be misused. Here the attendees of the Wübben Sandpit conference outline a defence-in-depth strategy that builds safeguards into every stage of sequence design.

item.title: Automated data to model transformation for constraint programming with AI
item.description:
Nature Communications · Zhengqi Shi, Jin Huang, Xinyu Li, Hao Zhang, Mingming Peng, Xinyi Yang
Artificial intelligence for combinatorial optimization depends on high-quality, structured training data, yet transforming ambiguous natural-language descriptions into precise, executable formal models remains a major bottleneck, traditionally requiring extensive manual effort and domain expertise. We develop CPAM-LLM, an automated constraint-programming modeling framework based on large language models that converts unstructured problem specifications into validated and executable formal models. The framework integrates retrieval-augmented generation grounded in formal concept analysis for structural validation, chaos-mapping-based data augmentation to enhance cross-domain generalization, and dynamic constraint adaptation to accommodate evolving problem settings. We demonstrate its effectiveness across five scenarios, including DNA sequence design, reconfigurable energy storage systems, and unmanned vehicle logistics. The results show that the framework can automate the data-to-model pipeline while adapting reliably to changing requirements, providing a practical approach to automated data formalization and indicating the importance of accessible, high-quality structured data for reliable downstream artificial intelligence applications.

item.title: An alternative path for artificial intelligence in Africa

item.title: Quantum-accurate vibrational and conformational dynamics from small molecules to proteins with machine-learned force fields
item.description:
Nature Communications · Sergio Suarez Dou, Miguel Gallegos, Kyunghoon Han, Florian N. Brünig, Joshua T. Berryman, Alexandre Tkatchenko
Abstract Biomolecular thermodynamics and spectroscopy depend on relative conformer energies, local curvatures, and collective dipole fluctuations on the potential-energy surface. Conventional molecular mechanics force fields enable large-scale simulations, but their fixed functional forms can misrepresent infrared intensities, mode character, and environment-dependent vibrational response. Here we assess general-purpose machine-learned force fields by using finite-temperature infrared spectra across small molecules, gas-phase peptides, and monomeric, oligomeric, and solvated protein assemblies. To enable this analysis, we introduce QVib, a dataset of 293 molecules and 1366 conformers, together with peptide amide-band benchmarks and p53 oligomerization-domain models, to evaluate vibrational transferability from DFT references to experimental spectra. Across these systems, machine-learned force fields improve over molecular mechanics in reproducing DFT-level forces, vibrational frequencies, densities of states, mode eigenvectors, conformational energetics, and experimental infrared spectra. Among models with explicit long-range electrostatics, SO3LR provides the best accuracy–cost balance of the models tested here. These results show that machine-learned force-field dynamics can recover collective, environment-dependent vibrational landscapes at near-DFT fidelity, enabling spectroscopically validated biomolecular simulations at force-field-like cost.

item.title: Supervised deep learning for efficient cryo-EM image alignment in drug discovery with cryoPARES
item.description:
Nature Communications · Rubén Sánchez-García, Alex Berndt, Amir Apelbaum, Judith Reeks, Pamela A. Williams, Carl R. Poelking
Cryo-Electron Microscopy (cryo-EM) is a pivotal tool for determining 3D structures of biological macromolecules. Current workflows are computationally demanding and require manual intervention, creating bottlenecks for high-throughput applications like structure-based drug discovery. In such contexts, where all protein samples can be assumed to be equivalent at resolutions relevant for image alignment, information about particle poses from previous refinements could be reused. Existing methods, however, ignore this prior knowledge, aligning each dataset from scratch. We present cryoPARES, a deep learning pose estimation method trained on pre-aligned datasets. Our method not only provides accurate angular predictions significantly faster than traditional approaches but also introduces automated particle pruning capabilities that eliminate manual intervention. Together with its single-pass operation, these features enable near real-time reconstructions that provide feedback during data acquisition. We demonstrate cryoPARES’s effectiveness through rapid structural determination of seven ligand-bound complexes across four distinct protein targets. We also release three fragment-bound cryo-EM datasets.

item.title: When AI-assisted criticism scales, peer review needs an obligation threshold

item.title: Machine learning-driven regulation of the four-electron LiOH pathway in lithium–oxygen batteries with prolonged cycling
item.description:
Nature Communications · 白天省, Yiming Hu, Wei Zhai, Xiongwei Zhong, Jinru Huang, Jiaxian Wang
Abstract The practical deployment of high-energy-density lithium–oxygen batteries is fundamentally restricted by sluggish oxygen redox kinetics and the instability of discharge intermediates. Here, we report an artificial intelligence-integrated framework leveraging interpretable machine learning and density functional theory to navigate a vast chemical space of thousands of active sites. This approach identifies Ni-Co dual-atom catalysts as a better configuration among the selected elements for orchestrating multi-electron transfer. Theoretical analysis reveals that synergistic electronic coupling between the dual-sites fundamentally reconfigures the d -band center, thereby lowering the thermodynamic barriers for oxygen redox. Moreover, the catalysts enable precise regulation of the reaction pathway, inducing a controllable transition from the conventional two-electron pathway to a four-electron pathway. This shift yields a discharge capacity of ~60,000 mAh g −1 . Beyond its role as a positive electrode catalyst, this architecture functions as a multifunctional interfacial protective layer that stabilizes the lithium metal negative electrode by suppressing dendrite growth. Consequently, the lithium–oxygen system achieves stable lifespan of 2075 cycles under the four-electron pathway with reduced voltage decay. This work establishes a data-guided strategy for the rational design of atomic-scale architecture via artificial intelligence, unlocking the potential of multi-electron oxygen chemistry for lithium–oxygen batteries.

item.title: Improving molecular property prediction with score-based diffusion models
item.description:
Nature Communications · Julien Horwood, Dino Oglić, José Miguel Hernández-Lobato
Abstract We explore diffusion-based training as a flexible approach to molecular property prediction in settings shaped by chemical, biophysical, and latent heterogeneity. To address this, we build on score-based generative diffusion models and introduce a conditional diffusion module for predictive tasks, equipped with a joint training and sampling guidance scheme and an optional gated residual mechanism that regulates feature- vs target-driven information flow across noise levels. The module acts as a plug-in learning block for existing molecular encoders, making it complementary to advances in representation learning. Across diverse feature extractors and graph neural networks, diffusion-based training improves over conventional maximum-likelihood objectives on small-molecule regression benchmarks and matches or exceeds strong baselines on multitask regression and classification datasets. It also produces well-calibrated predictive uncertainty as measured by prediction interval coverage, enables confidence-guided ranking, and performs well in challenging settings including activity cliffs and class-imbalanced multitask prediction. Overall, these results position diffusion as a promising representation-agnostic approach for effective molecular property prediction.
